podcast.title: Bringing High-Fidelity Recording to the West
podcast.body: Because the end of World War II invalidated all Nazi patents, Jack Mullin was able to take the newly discovered German reel-to-reel tape machines home. After leaving the army, he began demonstrating this previously unknown high-fidelity technology to potential investors in the West. This technological transfer laid the groundwork for modern studio recording techniques. "Because the war invalidated all Nazi patents, Moin was able to take the machine's home where, after getting out of the army, he started demonstrating this high fidelity technology that was unknown in the west for potential investors."

podcast.title: Discovery of Nazi Tape Recorders (World War II)
podcast.body: During World War II, as a major in the US Army Signal Corps, Jack Mullin stumbled upon two Nazi reel-to-reel tape recorders. These machines were used in German radio broadcasts to create confusion among the Allies regarding Adolf Hitler's whereabouts, as he could appear to be making multiple speeches simultaneously from different cities, thanks to pre-recorded tapes. Mullin was incredibly impressed by the high fidelity of the recordings, noting the absence of background noise and the indistinguishable quality between live and playback sound. "I'd never heard anything like that. As far to my knowledge, there just hadn't been anything like that anywhere in recording before. You couldn't tell whether it was live or playback."

podcast.title: Impact on Modern Recording Techniques
podcast.body: Along with investor Bing Crosby and guitarist Les Paul, Jack Mullin is credited with giving birth to modern recording studio techniques from the 1950s onward. His work with reel-to-reel tape made it possible for performances to be started, stopped, restarted, and edited with a razor blade and tape. Mistakes could be excised, jokes cut out, and overdubs became possible, allowing parts of a recording to be redone without affecting others. This also enabled the separate control of track volumes and the post-production addition of special effects like reverb and echo, transforming the studio into a musical instrument. "In short, Major Jack Moan, along with his early believer Bing Crosby and guitarist Les Paul, gave birth to modern recording studio techniques."

podcast.title: Pioneering Videotape Technology
podcast.body: The same tape recording technology introduced by Jack Mullin, initially developed for audio, also made videotape possible. This innovation completely transformed television broadcasting and, subsequently, home entertainment, showcasing the broad impact of Mullin's discoveries beyond just music. "And not only that, this same technology made videotape possible, and that completely transformed television and later home entertainment."

xref.title: Funding of Magnetic Tape Recorder (1940s)
xref.body: To solve the problem of broadcasting his radio show twice (once for the East Coast and three hours later for the West Coast), Bing Crosby invested $50,000 (over $600,000 in modern money) in Major Jack Mullin's magnetic tape machine. This investment allowed Mullin to perfect the Ampex 200 reel-to-reel tape recorder, which revolutionized radio broadcasting and music recording by enabling editing and time-shifting. "Bing was so interested in the new machine that he dropped $50,000 or more than $600,000 in today's money, so Mullen could perfect his machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Investment in Ampex and Tape Recording
xref.body: Bing Crosby became an investor in Ampex, an electronic firm that manufactured reel-to-reel machines based on Jack Mullin's German technology. Crosby was motivated by his dislike for having to repeat his national radio show for the West Coast time zone and saw tape recording as a solution to pre-tape his East Coast broadcast. His investment was crucial in developing modern studio techniques. "So Bing became an investor in Ampex, an electronic firm that had been making real-to-real machines based on Moin's German booty."
